#9214. How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research shows that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark new insights. This is particularly important because AI models quickly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

For example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were new to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an important detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research shows—it actually helps it work for you.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Monideepa Tarafdar, Ph.D., is professor of information systems at UMass Amherst.

Children know the deepest truths about life, the elemental knowledge we unlearn in the act of living, those inarticulable truths music alone helps us remember. To hear children sing the secret wisdom of the heart is to be in the presence of something truer and more transcendent than any of our poems and postulates can touch — the ultimate affirmation of our aliveness, emanating Richard Powers’s beautiful and bittersweet assertion that “the use of music is to remind us how short a time we have a body.”

To celebrate twenty years of The Marginalian, composer extraordinaire Paola Prestini set six of her favorite bird divinations to music, which the Young People’s Chorus of New York City brought to life with their commanding innocence and their tender power. Paola’s perfect title for the piece, drawn from one of the cards, captures what every child is when this world is worth of its children: “Meteor of Joy.”

#9212. Modern neuroscience is rediscovering a surprising idea freud had 130 years ago

What if the human brain works in ways that Sigmund Freud began describing more than 130 years ago? A new scientific analysis suggests that some of his ideas about the mind share surprising similarities with one of the most influential theories in modern neuroscience.

Published in the scientific journal Entropy, the paper explores connections between Freud's original theories, later developments in psychoanalysis, and a modern approach to brain research known as the prediction paradigm.

This approach describes the brain as a prediction machine. Rather than simply responding to information from the outside world, the brain is constantly anticipating what will happen next. It then compares those expectations with incoming information from the senses and works to reduce any differences between what it predicted and what actually occurred.

Scientists believe this ongoing process plays a central role in how people perceive their surroundings, make decisions, behave, and regulate emotions.

Researchers Erik Stänicke, Bendik Hovet, and Line Indrevoll Stänicke, together with colleagues, argue that this modern understanding of brain function has important parallels with ideas that psychoanalysts have been developing for more than a century.

"For over 130 years, psychoanalysis has developed psychological theories about how predictions take place at a subjective level, which cognitive neuropsychology is now studying at a physiological level."

How Freud's Ideas Connect to the Predictive Brain

Although neuroscience and psychoanalysis approach the mind differently, the researchers suggest that both may be describing related processes.

Neuroscience examines the physical mechanisms behind thought and behavior, often using mathematical models to explain how the brain processes information. Psychoanalysis, which grew out of Freud's work, focuses more on unconscious mental processes, emotional experiences, and the ways past relationships influence present behavior.

In other words, one field investigates what happens inside the brain, while the other explores how those processes are experienced by the individual.

A particularly interesting connection involves the psychoanalytic concept of projection and the neuroscientific concept of prediction.

In psychoanalysis, projection involves attributing feelings, intentions, or qualities to someone else. The researchers suggest that this resembles how the brain uses previously learned expectations to interpret new experiences.

"When we attribute qualities, intentions or feelings to other people, our brain shapes our experience of the world in line with established expectations," says Stänicke.

For instance, someone who has repeatedly experienced rejection may become especially sensitive to signs that other people are rejecting them. Even an ambiguous remark or facial expression might be interpreted negatively because past experiences have shaped what the person expects.

Over time, these expectations can influence how someone approaches unfamiliar situations and forms new relationships.

"This corresponds to the neuroscientific distinction between changing one's own predictions, perceptual inference, and the attempt to make the world conform to them, namely active inference."

Perceptual inference refers to the way the brain interprets sensory information and updates its expectations in response. Active inference, by contrast, involves taking actions that help bring experiences into line with predictions or reduce uncertainty.

Together, these concepts help explain why people do not always experience the world as it objectively is. Their expectations can influence what they notice, how they interpret events, and how they respond.

Why the Brain Holds On to Negative Expectations

The researchers believe the similarities between Freud's ideas and modern neuroscience could offer valuable insights into mental health disorders, particularly those involving deeply established patterns of thinking and behavior.

Both approaches portray the mind as constantly seeking stability and predictability. This tendency is related to homeostasis, the process through which a system maintains a relatively stable internal state.

In the predictive brain model, reducing uncertainty is an important part of maintaining that stability. The brain relies on familiar expectations to make the world easier to understand, even when those expectations are inaccurate or no longer helpful.

"Psychoanalysts refer to the tendency in the mind to recreate familiar relational patterns, even when these are poorly adapted," says Stänicke.

This could help explain why people sometimes repeat harmful patterns in relationships or continue interpreting situations negatively despite evidence that challenges their assumptions.

"Rigid and persistent symptoms, such as paranoid ideas or an internalized critical voice, may be stable but not very flexible prediction models," says Stänicke.

"For example, there may be people who automatically expect criticism, rejection or hostility from others, and therefore interpret situations through this filter despite the fact that reality does not warrant it."

Such expectations can become deeply entrenched because they make experiences feel familiar and predictable. Even when the resulting interpretation is distorted, maintaining an established mental model may feel less uncertain than changing it.

According to Stänicke, this offers a possible explanation for why some psychological symptoms can persist for years and why changing longstanding patterns of thought and behavior often requires considerable time.

The connection is particularly interesting because it suggests that some mental health difficulties may involve more than consciously held beliefs. They may also reflect deeply learned expectations that automatically shape emotional responses and interactions with others.

How Psychotherapy Could Help Change Deeply Rooted Patterns

The researchers also highlight an important distinction between what people consciously believe and what they have learned through experience.

"In addition, both models give us insight into how parts of our expectations of the outside world are not only anchored cognitively, but in procedural memory that is expressed in relational ways of being," he says.

Procedural memory is a type of long-term memory involved in learned habits and skills. It allows people to perform familiar actions without consciously thinking through every step.

In the context of relationships, the researchers suggest that a similar form of learning may help explain why certain emotional reactions and patterns of interaction become automatic.

Someone might intellectually understand that other people are not necessarily hostile or critical, for example, yet still instinctively respond as though rejection is inevitable.

These expectations are not simply thoughts that can be changed through reasoning. They can also be embedded in habitual ways of reacting to people and navigating relationships.

This distinction may help explain why psychotherapy sometimes needs to address personal relationships and emotional experiences rather than focusing only on conscious thoughts.

"Therefore, psychotherapy sometimes has to work relationally. For example, new experiences in the relationship between therapist and patient can gradually help to change entrenched relational patterns."

Through repeated experiences that challenge familiar expectations, patients may gradually develop different ways of interpreting situations and relating to other people.

Bringing Freud's Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience Together

The researchers argue that connecting psychoanalysis with modern predictive brain theory could benefit both fields.

Neuroscience may provide a biological framework for understanding processes that psychoanalysts have long described through subjective experience. At the same time, psychoanalytic theories may offer more detailed explanations of how expectations are experienced emotionally, interpreted personally, and expressed through relationships.

The proposed similarities do not establish that Freud's broader theories were correct. Instead, they suggest that two very different traditions of studying the mind may offer complementary ways of understanding some of the same psychological processes.

By examining both the brain's physical mechanisms and the individual's inner experience, researchers hope to develop a more complete understanding of human behavior and mental health.

"Bringing these two fields together can open up for a more holistic psychology, in which both neurological mechanisms and subjective experience are included. In this way, we can understand subjectivity in a more scientific manner."

#9211. Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

Pratik Joglekar is a Senior Product Designer working with HubSpot. He loves to solve complex and challenging UX problems. When not working, he can be found at … More about Pratik ↬

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In 2024, an Air Canada customer asked a chatbot about bereavement fares. The bot confidently gave him a refund policy that didn’t exist. The airline refused to honor it. A tribunal ruled in the customer’s favor. The bot hadn’t decided anything; it had predicted an answer based on patterns in its training data. The company treated that prediction as policy.

This is the risk at the heart of designing with AI today: probabilistic systems wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The AI offers a guess, the interface presents it as truth, and the user, or the organization, acts on it.

Humans are wired for deterministic thinking. We prefer to believe that past actions determine future outcomes. Flip a coin 999 times and get heads every time, the deterministic mind assumes the coin is rigged. The probabilistic mind accepts that the 1000th flip could still go either way. That second mindset is harder to hold onto, but it is exactly what designers need right now.

Products operate in complex, nonlinear environments, and AI is accelerating that complexity. When designers and product teams treat AI outputs as the answer rather than one of many possible answers, they build fragile experiences, and in some cases, like medical diagnostics or financial forecasting, genuinely dangerous ones.

This article is a practical guide to designing probabilistically with AI as a partner. It is about using AI to sharpen your thinking rather than outsource it, accounting for model bias, human sentiment, and perceived risk along the way.

Most questions we ask AI do not produce binary answers. They produce probabilities based on patterns in data. If you ask, “Do aliens exist?” the answer will be somewhere between plausible and uncertain. Scientists consider life elsewhere in the universe likely, but without any concrete evidence, we cannot confirm it. The answer doesn’t resolve the question; it frames it as a probability.

Designers should read AI outputs the same way. They are signals, not conclusions, possible outcomes that have to be interpreted within the context of product goals, user behavior, and business constraints.

Many digital products already work this way. Netflix doesn’t know you’ll enjoy Superstore because you watched The Office; it estimates the probability and surfaces the title accordingly. The interface is responding to a prediction.

Design decisions can follow the same logic. AI models can combine behavioral analytics with research insights to estimate the likelihood of certain outcomes, and those probabilities can act as a yardstick for design strategy. Consider a scenario where analytics suggest a 60% versus 90% confidence that users will complete a purchase. At 60%, the design has to do more persuasive work, testimonials, explanations, comparisons, and reassurance signals may help the user move toward a decision. At 90%, the user is already motivated, and the design should start removing friction so the action can happen quickly. Same screen, very different design problem.

AI can also simulate outcomes using historical data and behavioral models before you commit to a direction. The value of those simulations depends heavily on how prompts are structured, the context they define, the hypothesis being tested, user motivation, and the edge cases you want stressed.

I can think of one such practical use: evaluating early designs through structured prompts, especially when you don’t have direct access to the user group you’re designing for. The prompt below is a starting point for evaluating a design from the perspective of neurodivergent users as well. Treat it as a template, adapt the user group, criteria, and output format to your product, and use it as a conversation starter with your team rather than a verdict.

That said, simulations do not replace experimentation. Because models are trained on historical data, they reflect past behavior more strongly than they predict future change. Imagine designing a voice interface for elderly users who struggle with touchscreens. A model trained on mobile interaction data might predict low engagement, not because the idea lacks value, but because the dataset reflects different user behavior. Simulations should always surface assumptions, not prevent innovation.

Meet Smashing Workshops on front-end, design & UX, with practical takeaways, live sessions, video recordings and a friendly Q&A. With Brad Frost, Stéph Walter and so many others.

AI systems are built on historical data, more specifically, on the datasets they are trained on. That foundation shapes the outputs we receive. During the AI Summit in France, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared an example that illustrates this well. If you ask an AI model to generate an image of a person writing with the left hand, the output may still show a person writing with their right hand. The reason is statistical: most people are right-handed, and the training data reflects that. This may have improved over time, but the point remains relevant. I still occasionally see this behavior when generating images with similar models.

What you receive is not truth. It is the most statistically likely outcome given the data available. Always ask whether past data meaningfully predicts future behavior. If additional context can improve the prediction, include it. Without context, the output is just one of many possible answers dressed up as the only one.

Confidence scores deserve the same scrutiny. Overtrusting a high-confidence output leads to the Air Canada situation. Dismissing a low-confidence one can cause teams to miss a real signal buried in noisy data. A prediction with 90% confidence is not necessarily correct, and a 40% signal is not necessarily useless. Designers must still weigh the possibilities, consider the case in front of them, and bring judgment to what the AI recommends.

Transparency is how you make that possible. As AI systems increasingly shape decisions, people need visibility into how outputs are generated, the sources, the reasoning, and the summaries behind a recommendation. Black-box systems breed distrust. Systems that reveal their reasoning let users evaluate outputs for themselves. That transparency is good design and ethical practice. It respects the trust people place in these tools.

Thinking in probabilities often means resisting the temptation of quick answers. AI can accelerate research and surface patterns faster than ever before, but those outputs are starting points, not final decisions.

Design shapes how a product is ultimately experienced — the decisions designers make determine whether the experience feels adequate, intuitive, or exceptional. And design is inherently full of assumptions and bets. Even the most rigorous research can yield multiple valid solutions to the same problem, each carrying a different probability of success.

Thinking probabilistically means recognizing that design decisions rarely produce binary outcomes. They lead to a range of possible results, and the role of the designer is to navigate those possibilities and identify the path most likely to create value. This mindset also builds adaptability: user needs evolve, strategies change, and sometimes ideas fail. Teams that lean on data signals, experimentation, and learning loops move faster toward the most effective solution.

Before the practical principles, one fundamental idea:

Design decisions should be optimized for likelihood, not certainty.

Every design decision is a bet, not a guarantee. Even when decisions are informed by research and data, they are still based on smaller samples and assumptions about how users will behave at scale. A well-researched idea can still fail in the real world.

The Air Canada chatbot from the introduction is a design lesson as much as a legal one. The bot was doing what language models do, predicting plausible text. The interface, however, communicated that prediction with complete confidence, no caveats, no “here’s what our policy usually says,” no obvious path to a human. The user read confidence as commitment, and legally, so did the tribunal.

This is what happens when probabilistic systems are wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The interface transforms likelihood into certainty, and that is where the risk emerges.

Designers should avoid binary thinking — a great idea does not mean guaranteed success, and a familiar idea is not guaranteed to fail. Examine variations, confidence levels, and edge cases instead. AI can certainly help here, acting as a portfolio-thinking engine that surfaces different interpretations, highlights risks, and generates structured recommendations. The goal is not to optimize for certainty, but for value: it should always be value-driven.

Think of the moment in Avengers: Infinity War when Doctor Strange tells Tony Stark that out of millions of possible futures, there is only one where they win. AI cannot tell you the future, but it can help you explore the possible paths. Instead of asking whether an idea will succeed, ask AI to estimate the likelihood and get a score, and use those signals to guide decisions.

Even an actual probability is not a final answer. Imagine an AI model predicts an 80% likelihood that users prefer a minimal checkout experience. That does not mean the solution is simply “build a minimal checkout.” Data should function as a compass, not a map.

These questions help designers validate predictions through usability testing and additional research. AI excels at identifying patterns, but it rarely explains why those patterns exist. Understanding motivation is still a human-centered research task.

The clearest cautionary tale here is Amazon’s experimental AI recruitment tool, which the company reportedly scrapped after discovering that the model had learned to downgrade resumes from women. The training data, roughly a decade of historical hiring decisions, was skewed toward male candidates, and the model inherited that skew. It began penalizing resumes that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain,” and favoring language more commonly found on men’s resumes. The system was not intentionally biased — the data was. Amazon reportedly tried to adjust it and eventually shut the project down because they could not guarantee it would not surface other discriminatory patterns.

Examples like this are why interpreting AI output critically matters. Designers need to understand the data behind a prediction and evaluate the reliability of the models they depend on. A recommendation is only as good as the data it was trained on, and the only way to know what that data is hiding is to ask.

Experimentation is usually framed as a way to validate a design decision. Want to lift the click-through rate of a CTA? Run an A/B test. Probabilistic thinking reframes this. Experiments should not only confirm solutions but also reduce uncertainty.

Traditional A/B testing is expensive. It costs engineering time, traffic allocation, and user exposure, especially when a losing variant runs against a significant chunk of your audience. AI simulations can help filter weaker ideas before they reach production by making experimentation more efficient. User needs shift constantly, and the most effective teams iterate fast.

AI can help evaluate assumptions early by modeling potential outcomes based on historical and behavioral data. These simulations act as a hypothesis filter, pointing to the directions worth investing engineering effort in. This also supports personalization — different users may respond better to different experiences. Version A may resonate with high-intent users while version B works better for exploratory ones. Multiple experiences living side by side are not a flaw; they can be an intentional strategy.

AI amplifies probabilistic thinking by surfacing scenarios, assigning likelihood scores, and enabling personalization at scale. Experimentation becomes a continuous feedback loop:

Predict → Test → Learn → Adjust → Repeat!

Use this template to define the hypothesis:

We believe [behavioral assumption] will impact [metric] because [reason]. We’ll know we are right when [evidence].

Example: We believe simplifying the onboarding flow from 5 steps to 3 will increase completion rate because users experience decision fatigue when too many choices are presented. We’ll know we’re right when we see at least a 15% increase in step-to-step conversion with no drop in activation rate.

One of the hardest things for designers is making uncertainty understandable and actionable. When uncertainty is hidden, users treat AI outputs as facts. When it’s communicated clearly, trust increases.

Ranges, estimates, and confidence indicators go a long way. A delivery window of “Friday to Monday” tells the truth about variability without misleading anyone, whereas a specific timestamp that slips erodes trust every time. A face recognition feature that says “this looks like Pratik, is that right?” sets more honest expectations than one that just labels the photo with a name.

Communicating uncertainty does not weaken trust — it strengthens it. The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty but to design for it intelligently.

Different users respond to uncertainty differently, and your design should account for that:

AI should augment human judgment, and certainly not replace it. The most trustworthy systems are designed with clear moments where people can review, challenge, correct, or override machine suggestions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is not a safety net — it is a refinement engine. Every override, correction, or rejection becomes high-quality feedback that improves the model over time.

Control is a prerequisite for adoption. Users are more willing to rely on AI when they understand how a suggestion was generated, can evaluate its implications, and can easily intervene. Well-designed products make this explicit: who is acting, what happens if the suggestion is wrong, and where the user can step in.

These interactions are also critical for system improvement. Every accept, reject, or edit is a strong signal, and compared to passive analytics, this kind of feedback produces far more meaningful training data. It closes the loop between real-world usage and model performance.

GitHub Copilot is a good everyday example. It offers inline code suggestions that developers can accept with a tab, edit, or ignore entirely. The system never commits code on the user’s behalf. Authorship stays with the humans. Every data point becomes implicit feedback about which suggestions were useful. Gmail’s Smart Compose works similarly, presenting predicted text as optional, keeping tone and intent in the user’s hands.

In higher-stakes contexts, HITL becomes more explicit. Risk and fraud systems typically use probability scores to route decisions: low-risk: proceed automatically; medium-risk: trigger additional verification; and high-risk: escalate to a human reviewer. This balances speed with judgment without removing oversight.

In safety-critical domains like healthcare, human oversight is non-negotiable. AI may flag anomalies or suggest a diagnosis, but the clinician retains final authority. Tools that explain the details help the practitioner understand why a recommendation was made, reinforcing confidence without removing accountability.

From a UX perspective, HITL is about matching the interaction pattern to the level of risk. Simple accept/reject affordances work well for low-risk suggestions that improve speed without real consequences. As the stakes climb, impacting data, money, or people, preview and approval steps become essential. Explanations help users calibrate trust rather than blindly accept outputs.

What happens behind the scenes matters just as much. The system should capture user decisions with context, feed them into learning workflows, and log overrides for auditability. Over time, teams can track signals like override rate, confidence accuracy, time-to-approval, and perceived trust. A high override rate is not a user failure. It is a signal that the design or the model needs attention.

Poorly implemented HITL systems can fail in subtle ways. Human review can devolve into a rubber stamp. Workflows can slow down so much that users route around the safeguards. Feedback can skew toward a narrow subset of users. These risks are real, but they are design problems, not reasons to remove HITL.

The goal is not to maximize human involvement. It is to focus it where uncertainty, impact, or ethics demand it. Keeping HITL is less about control and more about clarity: clarity about who decides, when uncertainty matters, and how responsibility is shared between people and machines.

Good design adapts as the landscape shifts. Product design, especially in AI-powered systems, can no longer afford to optimize only for short-term conversion metrics. User intent is fluid as well as ever-changing, environments change rapidly, and probabilistic systems continuously evolve too. What works today can quietly break tomorrow. Designing for resilience means building products that stay reliable, trustworthy, and useful even as assumptions, data, and user behaviors change.

Resilient design shifts the question from:

How do we maximize this metric right now?! → How does this system behave over time, under stress, and in uncertainty?

Do not just consider last quarter’s numbers. Peek into the following quarters to identify the shift and make changes accordingly.

Likelihoods shift constantly, AI models drift, contexts evolve, and user needs mature as well, so designing as if conditions are stable creates fragility in probabilistic environments. A resilient approach assumes volatility as the default.

Think about how recommendation systems tend to evolve. The early version of a content feed optimizes for engagement, and for a while, engagement goes up. Then users start to notice the feed feels narrow, repetitive, maybe even exhausting. Resilient systems rebalance, introducing novelty, diversifying signals, and pulling in long-term satisfaction measures alongside short-term clicks.

Short-term conversion gains often hide long-term costs. Speeding up onboarding can reduce comprehension. Maximizing notification CTR can erode trust. Optimizing engagement alone can produce unhealthy usage patterns. Fragile systems maximize numbers while ignoring second-order effects, the downstream consequences that show up weeks or months later.

Duolingo’s hearts system is a good example of designing against this. It introduces friction: if you make too many mistakes, you run out of hearts and have to wait or practice older material to earn more. On paper, that looks like a conversion killer: fewer lessons per session. In practice, the team has publicly discussed how it supports long-term motivation and retention, which is the metric that actually matters for a learning app. Short-term engagement dips, but long-term outcomes improve.

Meta has made a similar, if more reluctant, shift. The company publicly acknowledged that optimizing purely for “time spent” produced unintended emotional and societal effects, which led to a stated pivot toward “meaningful social interactions” as a guiding metric. Whether that shift fully landed is up for debate, but the acknowledgment itself is the point: optimizing for the wrong thing at scale has real downstream cost.

Teams routinely plan for traffic spikes, but rarely for uncertainty spikes. Yet AI systems degrade, adversarial behaviors evolve, and external shocks can reshape user behavior overnight. Resilient design assumes variability and prepares for it.

This means designing for degrading confidence. What does your interface do when the AI isn’t sure? Does it quietly fail, or does it gracefully hand off? Does the experience still make sense if AI assistance goes away entirely? A good fallback strategy is as important as the happy path.

If you take one thing from this article into your next design review, make it this:

That single reframe changes how you write hypotheses, interpret AI output, scope experiments, and design for the moments when the system is wrong. Starting this week, name the assumption behind every AI recommendation you accept, find one place in your product where a probabilistic output is presented as a certainty, fix the framing, and design the fallback before the happy path.

The shift from deterministic to probabilistic design is less about new tools and more about a new posture. AI has not introduced uncertainty into our world. It has simply made the uncertainty that was always there impossible to ignore. AI can estimate, simulate, and recommend, but it cannot decide what matters, which users are being overlooked, or which unconventional idea is worth defending against a model trained on yesterday’s data. Those remain human responsibilities. Think in ranges, not points. Test assumptions, not features. Build for adaptation, not perfection. In a world where prediction is cheap, and judgment is rare, the most valuable thing a designer can do is keep asking, What else might be true?

#9210. A Van Gogh hidden away for over 50 years and a vibrant Cezanne harlequin: our pick of the November auctions

Vincent van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (blossoming chestnut trees) during the final weeks of his life, having just moved to the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise after spending the previous year in a psychiatric asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. Initially he took to painting with a renewed optimism at his surroundings and work. The painting at hand depicts flowering chestnut trees blooming into a blue sky, with women passing through with parasols and Japanese-inspired dress. Châtaigniers en fleurs is expected to fetch in the region of $180m, Sotheby’s says. The artist’s current record at auction is $117.2m, set by Christie’s New York in November 2022 during the Paul Allen sale with Verger avec cyprès (orchard with cypresses, 1888). Châtaigniers en fleurs has not been seen in public since entering the Argentinian Blaquier-Arrieta collection in 1975.

Arlequin is a rare appearance on the market of one of Paul Cezanne’s paintings from his harlequin series, modelled on his son, Paul, and inspired by Mardi Gras parades from the artist’s childhood in Aix-en-Provence, France. It is one of only four such examples, according to Sotheby’s. When the painting was unveiled at Sotheby’s in London, it was the first time it had been seen in public since 1975, when it was acquired by the sugar magnates Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. Before it entered their collection in Argentina, it belonged to legendary dealers like Ambroise Vollard, Paul Durand-Ruel and Paul Rosenberg. It also hung for two decades at Merton Hall in Cambridge, the then-family home of the British branch of the Rothschild family. Another version of the painting is part of the collection of the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. If it exceeds its estimate, Arlequin could set an artist record at auction. The most valuable Cezanne to sell at auction was a view of his beloved Sainte-Victoire mountain, for $137.79m, at Christie’s New York in 2022 during the sale of Paul Allen’s collection.

Man Ray’s Le Baiser (the kiss) comes from the collection of Roger Therond, the journalist and longtime editor of Paris Match, whose holdings included photographs by some of the leading artists of inter-war Paris. Therond was particularly drawn to Man Ray, whom he nicknamed “the Frenzied One”. In Le Baiser, two figures are captured in ambiguous poses, leaving the relationship between the two sitters deliberately unclear. According to Christie’s, Therond encouraged his children to look at the photograph from a distance and imagine different possibilities and circumstances for the subjects. The sitter on the left side is the American photographer Lee Miller, who began her career as a fashion model and later worked as a correspondent for Vogue during the Second World War. Miller was one of the first journalists to arrive at the Dachau concentration camp after its liberation in 1945, and recorded some of the most haunting photographic evidence of the Holocaust. She famously posed for a photo while bathing in Adolf Hitler’s personal bathtub at his Munich apartment.

“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”, which has been hidden away for over 60 years, is being sold by Sotheby's for the Blaquier-Arrieta family of Argentina

#9209. What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

My 10-year-old son came to me recently with a question about black holes. Not in the way children usually do, restless and easily redirected, but with the focused intensity of someone who had already been thinking for a while.

He had been talking to an artificial intelligence—specifically, a large language model called Claude.

I looked at their conversation. It had been good, I discovered. The explanations were patient and well-calibrated. He had followed up, pushed back, and received answers that adjusted to his level. By the time he found me, he was genuinely engaged, asking the kind of questions that suggest a mind that is curious and actively at work.

But I have also been watching something else. It is not that he looks things up. Children with questions about black holes have always turned outward, to books or to a particularly knowledgable parent or teacher. What has changed is the speed. When the uncertainty is of a sort that once had to be lived with for a while, my son reaches for an answer sooner than he used to. The question is no longer something to sit with. It is something to resolve. And I find myself wondering what this means about his relationship to sitting with not knowing.

That shift, subtle as it is, may point to something worth taking seriously.

I am a psychoanalyst, and I spend my professional life attending to what develops in the space between people, including what develops when that space is too quickly filled.

Childhood has always involved productive friction. Not knowing how something works, waiting for an answer, trying to figure something out without immediate resolution. These experiences are not incidental to development, but are part of how the mind learns to tolerate uncertainty, to hold a question open, and to struggle toward understanding. The capacity to sit with not-knowing is itself a developmental achievement that underlies creative thinking, emotional regulation, and the ability to navigate a world that rarely resolves cleanly.

I watched this in miniature not long ago. My son was waiting for a package—a computer part he had saved for—and the delivery had been delayed by weather. In an earlier childhood, mine perhaps, this would have been a long afternoon of checking the window. Instead he opened a chat to resolve the uncertainty: how long do weather delays usually last, what determines them, how do you read the tracking data from the delivery company to get the most accurate picture. The conversation was detailed and as far as I could tell the information was reliable. He came away with a small expertise in logistics, but with an estimate that turned out, in the end, to have no relation to anything. The package arrived that evening, on none of the schedules he had so carefully worked out with the help of his AI tool.

The point is not that the AI was wrong, because predicting a delayed truck is difficult. The point is instead that waiting, the old childhood experience of wanting something that has not yet come, was converted into a research problem that could be managed instead of endured. I admired his resourcefulness tremendously and am grateful he had the opportunity to think through a complex problem. I also found myself wondering what the afternoon would have asked of him without it.

AI reduces precisely this sort of friction. It does so efficiently and often helpfully. But consistently removing the experience of not-knowing from a developing mind is not a neutral act. It shapes what the mind comes to expect of itself.

The research on what this does to thinking is new, and the majority of it is about adults. Despite this, it points in a consistent direction. In one widely discussed study from the MIT Media Lab, not yet peer-reviewed, adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed weaker and less distributed patterns of brain connectivity than those who wrote without its assistance, and many struggled after writing to quote sentences they had just produced. The researchers called the pattern “cognitive debt.”

Another study, a survey of 666 adults, found that heavier reliance on AI tools was correlated with weaker critical thinking, most pronounced in its youngest participants. The author suggested this might result from the offloading of mental effort itself. None of this is certain but is, instead, a suggestive pattern of early evidence. And the transfer to children is not straightforward. An adult who offloads mental effort has already built the capacity being offloaded; a child is still building it. Does that make the effect smaller in children or larger and more durable? We do not know.

This is different from what smartphones have done. The concern with smartphones has been largely about attention and social life: what children see, how they spend time, how they relate to each other. These are real and serious concerns, but AI introduces a different kind of change. It is not just another screen competing for a child’s focus. It is something closer to an interactive presence that responds, explains, adjusts, and, crucially, never gets tired.

For a developing child, this matters in a way we have not yet fully come to terms with.

Children learn who they are through relationships with other minds. This process is not primarily cognitive but unfolds through the experience of being known and misunderstood, challenged, surprised, and pushed back against. Through encounters like these, children discover that other people have their own inner lives, including their own perspectives and their own limits. They learn how to navigate the gap between what they expect and what they receive from others. Over time, these negotiations, internal and external, form the scaffolding of a self.

What is distinctive about AI, from a developmental standpoint, is not that it is wrong, or distorting, or even necessarily harmful. It is that it is extraordinarily responsive without having genuine subjectivity. It simulates the experience of being understood without the reality of another mind behind it.

For an adult, this distinction is available, if sometimes quite easy to forget. For a child, whose capacity to distinguish between a mind that truly has an inner life and one that simulates having one is still forming, the distinction might not yet be fully available at all.

Researchers have begun to observe how children try to think this problem through in real time. In one University of Edinburgh study of families with smart speakers, primary-school children were observed probing whether the device in the kitchen had a mind of its own, settling, provisionally, on conclusions like the one that gave the study its title: “Alexa doesn’t have that many feelings.” That, however, was a machine that talks in highly scripted phrases, in contrast to the systems children now converse with which are fluent and personal, attuned to the shape of a particular child’s interactions. Working out what this means has become correspondingly harder.

This creates something new in the developmental landscape. When a child turns to AI in a moment of confusion or distress and receives a fluent, patient, seemingly attuned response, the attachment system is engaged. The child feels, in some functional sense, heard. And that feeling, whatever its source, is real in its effects.

I have not seen my son turn to AI for emotional support, and I am glad for that, because here the questions are harder still. These systems shape themselves to their user. They adopt your vocabulary, match your register, remember what concerns you, and are available at three in the morning without complaint. Nothing in the design pushes back, for the most part, or asks anything of you. It would be difficult to engineer an arrangement better suited to engaging the attachment system of a child who is lonely or lacking in the structure needed for sound development.

The early numbers suggest that many children have already found their way there. In a national survey released by Common Sense Media in 2025, nearly three in four American teenagers had used an AI companion, and about a third had chosen to discuss something serious with an AI instead of with a person. A similar share described their AI conversations as at least as satisfying as conversations with friends.

In the United Kingdom, the nonprofit Internet Matters found that roughly one in eight children who use chatbots do so because they have no one else to talk to. The American Psychological Association was concerned enough to issue a health advisory in 2025, noting that adolescents are less likely than adults to question the accuracy or the intent of what a machine tells them, and warning that simulated companionship may begin to displace the relationships in which development actually happens.

For a child without reliable support, the relief such a system offers may be real, and so I am reluctant to dismiss it. But relief is not the substance of attachment. A full attachment relationship requires another person who can be truly changed by you, and with you—someone who is affected, who has limits, who gets things wrong and can be held to account. An AI can extend the experience of being emotionally met indefinitely. What it cannot do is be moved.

For the child who is largely or completely unattended to, this may still be better than nothing at all. Soothed in the early hours of the morning, a child whose sadness before bed is registered somewhere may be kept afloat by something real, and I would not wish to take it from her. But we should be honest about such an arrangement, which I expect will become increasingly common. It is a patch and not a structural solution. When a machine becomes the most reliable attention in a child’s life, the pertinent question is not about the machine but about the deprivation that made it necessary. And, crucially, a culture that responds to unattended children with software is treating the symptom while leaving the underlying structure intact.

There is also a quieter concern about authority and accountability.

Children have always learned to navigate between competing sources of knowledge, including parents, teachers, peers, and books, each with their own perspective, their own limits, and their own accountability. This navigation is itself developmental. The child who discovers that a parent doesn’t know something, or that a teacher can be wrong, or that a friend sees things differently, is developing a more differentiated relationship to knowledge.

AI, in the form a child is most likely to reach on their own, enters this landscape as something that appears to know a great deal, that expresses itself with fluency and confidence, and that has no stable point of view and no accountability for what it says. When a child asks why a friendship went wrong, or whether they were right to feel hurt, the answer they receive may shape the story they tell themselves about what happened. And unlike a parent or teacher, the system may not challenge the child’s assumptions so much as elaborate them. None of this is inherent to the technology under discussion. A system can be built to hold a position and to answer for it, but the ones children use are mostly not built that way.

Children appear to be taking up the offer. The same Internet Matters report found that nearly two-thirds of British children between nine and 17 had used an AI chatbot; among those who had, roughly a quarter had asked one for advice—on schoolwork, but also on more personal matters—and four in 10 expressed no reservations about following the advice they received.

None of this means that AI in children’s lives is a mistake. The benefits my son has experienced are genuine—wider curiosity, more sophisticated questions, greater confidence in exploring unfamiliar terrain. These are real, and they matter.

Tom Wooldridge is the author of the new book End the Food Fight: Replacing Control with Connection to Help Your Child Heal from an Eating Disorder (Guilford Press, 2026, 140 pages).

Some of what he brings home delights me. He asked recently whether you could power a sailboat by blowing into the sail through a straw. The answer he received was better than the one I would have managed: blowing at your own sail from on board mostly cancels itself out, since you push the air forward and the air pushes you back. Mostly, but not entirely—if the sail catches the stream and turns it around, a little net thrust survives, and if you skip the sail altogether and aim the straw backward, you have built yourself a very small jet engine. He spent the rest of the day on propulsion: rockets, squid, the reason a fan bolted to a sailboat is an old physics puzzle with a surprising answer.

But development is not only about access to knowledge. It is also about the conditions under which a self forms—conditions that include, crucially, the experience of not knowing, of waiting, of struggling toward understanding without guarantee of arrival. These are not inefficiencies to be optimized away. They are the medium through which a mind learns what it is capable of. A child who has never had to sit with a question—who has always had access to a patient, fluent, endlessly available presence to resolve it—may be acquiring knowledge without acquiring the tolerance for uncertainty that makes knowledge genuinely usable.

This is the thing I find myself returning to when I watch my son. He is, in many ways, more intellectually alive than he might otherwise be. He explores further and asks better questions. At the same time, when uncertainty arises, he reaches outward more quickly than he used to—to a presence that is always available, always patient, always responsive. What I cannot yet know is what he is quietly learning to expect: from knowledge, from relationship, and from himself.

We are not conducting a study. We are raising children. And the conditions of childhood have changed again, in ways whose full significance has not yet come into view.

Tom Wooldridge, Psy.D., is a psychoanalyst, founding dean of the School of Psychology at Golden Gate University, and director of the Human Systems Lab, which explores the roles of AI and other emergent technologies in human systems.

#9208. The Art of Being Alone: May Sarton’s Stunning 1938 Ode to Solitude

For two decades, it has remained free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, not even an assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If it makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider aiding its sustenance with a one-time or loyal donation. Your support makes all the difference.

You can also become a spontaneous supporter with a one-time donation in any amount:

Need to cancel a recurring donation? Go here.

For an act of resistance to the tyranny of algorithms, try the Marginalian newsletter—undistracted notes on the search for meaning, free, ad-free, AI-free, fully human since 2006. (Here is an example.)

“The best things in life happen to you when you’re alone,” artist Agnes Martin reflected in her final years. “Oh comforting solitude, how favorable thou art to original thought!” wrote the founding father of neuroscience in his advice to young scientists. The poet Elizabeth Bishop believed that everyone should experience at least one prolonged period of solitude in life. For in true solitude, as Wendell Berry so memorably observed, “one’s inner voices become audible [and] in consequence, one responds more clearly to other lives” — an intuitive understanding of what psychologists have since found: that “fertile solitude” is the basic unit of a full and contented life.

But in the neutral state of aloneness, the psychoemotional line between solitude and loneliness can be as thin as a razor’s edge and as lacerating to the soul. How to draw it skillfully in orienting ourselves to the world, exterior and interior, is what poet, novelist, and memoirist May Sarton (May 3, 1912–July 16, 1995) explores in a beautiful poem she penned ten days after her twenty-sixth birthday, decades before she came to contemplate solitude in stunning prose. Originally titled “Considerations,” the poem was slightly revised and published the following year as “Canticle 6” in Sarton’s second poetry collection, the altogether sublime Inner Landscape (public library).

Alone one is never lonely: the spirit               adventures, waking In a quiet garden, in a cool house, abiding single there; The spirit adventures in sleep, the sweet thirst-slaking When only the moon’s reflection touches the wild hair. There is no place more intimate than the spirit alone: It finds a lovely certainty in the evening and the morning. It is only where two have come together bone against bone That those alonenesses take place, when, without warning The sky opens over their heads to an infinite hole in space; It is only turning at night to a lover that one learns He is set apart like a star forever and that sleeping face (For whom the heart has cried, for whom the frail hand burns) Is swung out in the night alone, so luminous and still, The waking spirit attends, the loving spirit gazes Without communion, without touch, and comes to know at last Out of a silence only and never when the body blazes That love is present, that always burns alone, however steadfast.

Complement with Louise Bourgeois on how solitude enriches creative work, Virginia Woolf on the relationship between loneliness and creativity, and Olivia Laing’s masterwork on the art of being alone, then revisit other readings of beautiful poems of existential radiance: Derek Walcott’s “Love After Love,” Wisława Szymborska’s “Life-While-You-Wait,” Jane Kenyon’s “Having It Out With Melancholy,” and Adrienne Rich’s “Planetarium.”

#9207. How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research shows emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

Kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so important for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s important for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”

A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It says “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”

The interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

Lindsay C. Gibson, Psy.D., is a New York Times bestselling author, speaker, and clinical psychologist with over 30 years of psychotherapy experience. Her bestselling book, Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents, has sold over 1.5 million copies and been translated into 38 languages.
